claims.text: Maintaining transition-metal surface active sites in an intermediate oxidation state enhances catalytic activity, selectivity, and durability.
The surface oxidation state can be tuned by adjusting oxygen partial pressure.
High-entropy oxide or high-entropy alloy catalyst surfaces exhibit mixed oxidation states.
The proportion of metal ions in intermediate oxidation states governs the catalyst's electronic structure.
A balanced Co3+/Co2+ ratio is an example of the proposed intermediate oxidation-state distribution.
Changing oxygen partial pressure shifts the catalyst's surface oxidation state.
Changing transition-metal oxidation state modulates the d-band electronic structure.
Modulation of the d-band electronic structure changes the binding of reaction intermediates.
An intermediate oxidation state optimizes, rather than merely strengthens, the binding energies of reaction intermediates.
Optimized adsorption and desorption dynamics increase catalytic activity and selectivity.
The proposed electronic and adsorption tuning also improves catalyst durability.
An intermediate oxygen-partial-pressure range will produce intermediate oxidation-state distributions.
Catalysts at intermediate oxygen partial pressure will outperform catalysts under fully oxidizing or reducing conditions in activity, selectivity, and durability.
Without deliberate oxygen-partial-pressure modulation, catalyst oxidation states remain relatively static.
The proposed relationship should hold for transition-metal catalysts operating at 300–400°C in industrially relevant redox-active environments.
The proposed relationship may not apply to non-oxide catalysts or catalysts operating through fundamentally different mechanisms.
XAS can quantify mixed divalent and trivalent oxidation states in these materials.
Absence of a correlation between intermediate oxidation-state fraction and performance, or peak performance outside an intermediate oxidation-state profile, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The initial material scope explicitly includes high-entropy alloys, which are commonly non-oxide catalysts, while the boundary states that the hypothesis may not apply to non-oxide catalysts.

The main hypothesis is phrased as applying generally to transition-metal catalysts, whereas the boundary narrows applicability to elevated-temperature, redox-active environments and potentially excludes non-oxide systems.
